## RStudio Projects

<p class="question">An RStudio Project is a folder-based workspace.</p>

What it does:

- marks the workshop folder as one self-contained project
- opens RStudio in the correct working directory

Why it matters:

- paths start from the project folder
- scripts, data, slides, and exercises stay together

For this workshop, open the provided R project file.

## Why Projects Matter

With the project open, these paths work:

```{r eval=FALSE}
read_csv("workshop_module/data/chinese_ldt.csv")
```

Without the project open, R may look in the wrong folder.

Check your current project folder:

```{r eval=FALSE}
getwd()
```

## Download The Workshop Folder

Later, participants can download the workshop module from GitHub.

```{r eval=FALSE}
workshop_url <- "https://github.com/USERNAME/REPOSITORY/archive/refs/heads/main.zip"
zip_file <- "lplus-2026-ws.zip"

download.file(workshop_url, zip_file, mode = "wb")
unzip(zip_file)

file.rename(
  "REPOSITORY-main/workshop_module",
  "workshop_module"
)
```

Then open `workshop_module/lplus-2026-ws.Rproj`.

## Creating A Project

For your own work later:

- **File > New Project**
- choose **New Directory** or **Existing Directory**
- keep raw data in a `data/` folder
- keep scripts in a `scripts/` or `exercises/` folder
- open the `.Rproj` file before working

Project paths should be relative:

```{r eval=FALSE}
read_csv("data/my_data.csv")
```

## Why Preprocess Data?

Problem:

- data rarely arrive in the shape needed for analysis

Goal:

- preprocessing turns raw data into analysable data

Scripts make data processing reproducible and reduce manual spreadsheet edits.

## The Tidyverse

Collection of R packages that share:

- common data structures
- common function style
- common assumptions about tidy data
- tools designed to work together

```{r eval=FALSE}
install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)
```

## Tidy Data

```{r echo=FALSE, out.width="80%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("assets/tidy_1.png")
```

- Each variable has its own column
- Each observation has its own row
- Each value has its own cell

## One Shared Pattern

<p class="question">Most tidyverse data processing functions follow one logic.</p>

```{r eval=FALSE}
verb(data, instructions)
```

Examples:

```{r eval=FALSE}
select(data, variable)
filter(data, variable > 100)
mutate(data, new_variable = old_variable * 2)
summarise(data, mean_variable = mean(variable))
```

## More Variables

The data also contain useful predictors and item information.

Task variables:

- `ppt_id`, `trial`, `stimulus`, `script`, `lexicality`
- `word_eng`, `response`, `correct_response`

Outcome variables:

- `rt`, `rt_sec`, `correct`

The data also include `device` and `browser` from the online task export.

## Reading CSV Files

```{r eval=FALSE}
chinese_ldt_base <- read.csv("workshop_module/data/chinese_ldt.csv")
class(chinese_ldt_base)
# "data.frame"
```

Base R returns a data frame. `read_csv` returns a tibble.

```{r eval=FALSE}
chinese_ldt <- read_csv("workshop_module/data/chinese_ldt.csv")
class(chinese_ldt)
# "spec_tbl_df" "tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame"
```

## Reading Excel Files

```{r eval=FALSE}
library(readxl)

chinese_ldt_excel <- read_excel("workshop_module/data/chinese_ldt.xlsx")
```

Use this when collaborators send `.xlsx` files.

## Reading SPSS Files

```{r eval=FALSE}
library(haven)

chinese_ldt_spss <- read_sav("workshop_module/data/chinese_ldt.sav")
```

Use this when data come from SPSS.

## RStudio Import Dataset

For spreadsheet-style importing:

- Use **Import Dataset**
- Choose the file
- Check the preview
- Copy the generated code into your script

The non-code route is useful for discovery, but the generated code should still end up in the script.

## Inspect Before Changing

```{r eval=FALSE}
glimpse(chinese_ldt)
names(chinese_ldt)
count(chinese_ldt, lexicality)
```

Open `workshop_module/exercises/01_reading_inspecting.R`.

## Store The Result

Tidyverse functions return a new data frame.

```{r eval=FALSE}
select(chinese_ldt, ppt_id, stimulus, rt)
```

This shows the result, but does not save it.

```{r eval=FALSE}
chinese_ldt_small <- select(chinese_ldt, ppt_id, stimulus, rt)
```

This saves the result so the next line can use `chinese_ldt_small`.

## Selecting Variables

Keep only the variables you need.

```{r eval=FALSE}
select(chinese_ldt, ppt_id, stimulus, rt)
```

## Selecting Many Variables

```{r eval=FALSE}
select(chinese_ldt, ppt_id, stimulus, contains("response"))
```

## Dropping Variables

Use `-` inside `select` to remove variables.

```{r eval=FALSE}
select(chinese_ldt, -device, -browser, -rt_sec)
```

## Filtering Rows

Keep rows that match a condition.

```{r eval=FALSE}
filter(chinese_ldt, rt > 2000)
```

```{r eval=FALSE}
filter(chinese_ldt, lexicality == "word")
```

## Filtering With Multiple Conditions

```{r eval=FALSE}
filter(chinese_ldt, rt > 2000, lexicality == "word")
```

```{r eval=FALSE}
filter(chinese_ldt, lexicality %in% c("word", "nonword"))
```

## Missing Values

Missing values are `NA`, not `"NA"`.

```{r eval=FALSE}
filter(chinese_ldt, is.na(rt))
```

```{r eval=FALSE}
filter(chinese_ldt, !is.na(rt))
```

## Creating Variables

`mutate` adds or changes columns.

```{r eval=FALSE}
mutate(
  chinese_ldt,
  rt_sec = rt / 1000
)
```

## More Mutate Examples

```{r eval=FALSE}
mutate(
  chinese_ldt,
  correct = response == correct_response,
  slow_trial = rt > mean(rt)
)
```

Open `workshop_module/exercises/02_select_filter_mutate.R`.

## Descriptive Summaries

```{r eval=FALSE}
summarise(
  chinese_ldt,
  mean_rt = mean(rt),
  sd_rt = sd(rt),
  accuracy = mean(correct),
  n = n()
)
```

## Summaries By Group

Use `.by` for grouped summaries.

```{r eval=FALSE}
summarise(
  chinese_ldt,
  mean_rt = mean(rt),
  sd_rt = sd(rt),
  accuracy = mean(correct),
  n = n(),
  .by = lexicality
)
```

## Two Grouping Variables

```{r eval=FALSE}
summarise(
  chinese_ldt,
  mean_rt = mean(rt),
  accuracy = mean(correct),
  n = n(),
  .by = c(script, lexicality)
)
```

Open `workshop_module/exercises/03_summarise_by.R`.

## Integrated Exercise

Build a short preprocessing workflow:

1. Read with `read_csv`
2. Inspect with `glimpse`
3. Reduce with `select` and `filter`
4. Create with `mutate`
5. Summarise with `.by`

Open `workshop_module/exercises/04_integrated_live_exercise.R`.

## Optional Backup: Pivoting

Pivoting changes data shape.

```{r eval=FALSE}
chinese_ldt_summary <- summarise(
  chinese_ldt,
  mean_rt = mean(rt),
  accuracy = mean(correct),
  n = n(),
  .by = c(ppt_id, lexicality)
)
```

## Optional Pivot Wider

Create one row per participant, with separate columns for words and nonwords.

```{r eval=FALSE}
chinese_ldt_summary_wide <- pivot_wider(
  chinese_ldt_summary,
  names_from = lexicality,
  values_from = c(mean_rt, accuracy, n)
)
```

## Optional Pivot Longer

```{r eval=FALSE}
scores_long <- pivot_longer(
  chinese_ldt_summary,
  cols = c(mean_rt, accuracy),
  names_to = "measure",
  values_to = "value"
)
```

Optional pivoting exercise: `workshop_module/exercises/05_optional_pivoting_backup.R`.

## Apply This Workflow To Your Own Data

<div class="function-overview">

| Function | Use it for |
|---|---|
| `read_csv` / `read_excel` / `read_sav` | read common file formats into R |
| `glimpse` | inspect variable names and types before editing |
| `select` | keep or drop variables to make data more manageable |
| `filter` | remove errors, practice trials, or implausible responses |
| `mutate` | create or change variables needed for analysis |
| `summarise` + `.by` | turn trial-level data into grouped descriptive results |
| `pivot_wider` / `pivot_longer` | reshape data frame orientation |

</div>

\ 

A useful next step is pipe-based preprocessing workflows: `|>` or `%>%`
